title: 1 Samuel 13:8–15
context: 1 Samuel 13:8–15 is the first account of Saul’s failure and its consequences. Samuel had told him to wait seven days at Gilgal until he came to offer the sacrifices and give instructions (10:8). As the days run out and the army scatters, Saul offers the burnt offering himself. Samuel arrives just as he finishes, rebukes him, and announces that Saul’s kingdom will not continue: the LORD has sought “a man after his own heart” to be prince over his people. The judgment concerns Saul’s kingship and dynasty. Both traditions read it as a lesson about obedience to God’s word and the accountability of Israel’s king, not as a statement about Saul’s eternal destiny.

verses.text: He stayed seven days, according to the time set by Samuel; but Samuel didn’t come to Gilgal, and the people were scattering from him.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul waits seven days “according to the time set by Samuel,” but Samuel does not come, and the people scatter. Arminian readers note that Saul partly obeys, waiting the full period, and that the pressure of the moment was real. The narrative presents his test as a genuine choice between waiting on God’s word and acting on his own judgment.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note the instruction of 10:8: “Wait seven days, until I come to you and show you what you are to do.” The command included waiting for Samuel himself, not merely counting days. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the setting of a real test of obedience and trust, in which delay is part of what God allowed.

verses.text: Saul said, “Bring the burnt offering to me here, and the peace offerings.” He offered the burnt offering.
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says, “Bring the burnt offering to me here, and the peace offerings,” and offers the burnt offering. Arminian readers note that Saul acts to secure God’s favor before battle, but does so by taking a role that Samuel had reserved for himself. The act shows impatience overriding obedience, even though Saul’s wish to seek the LORD before battle was not wrong in itself.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers emphasize that God’s worship must follow his appointed order; good intentions do not justify setting aside his explicit word. Later, Uzziah is told, “It isn’t for you, Uzziah, to burn incense to the LORD” (2 Chronicles 26:18). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a breach of a specific command, whatever interpreters conclude about the precise role a king might play in sacrifice.

verses.text: It came to pass that as soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering, behold, Samuel came; and Saul went out to meet him, that he might greet him.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel arrives “as soon as he had finished offering the burnt offering.” Arminian readers note the painful timing. Had Saul waited only a little longer, the crisis would have passed. The detail highlights how one impatient decision can bring lasting loss.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence in the timing, which exposes Saul’s heart under pressure. Saul goes out to greet Samuel as if nothing were wrong. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as dramatic irony that underlines the importance of waiting on God’s timing, and both note Saul’s apparent unawareness of the gravity of his act.

verses.text: Samuel said, “What have you done?” Saul said, “Because I saw that the people were scattered from me, and that you didn’t come within the days appointed, and that the Philistines assembled themselves together at Michmash,
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel asks, “What have you done?” Saul explains that the people were scattering, Samuel had not come “within the days appointed,” and the Philistines were gathering. Arminian readers note that Saul’s reasons are understandable in human terms, but they place circumstance above the word of the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul shifts responsibility to the people, to Samuel’s delay, and to the enemy. His explanation focuses on what he saw rather than on what God commanded. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the human tendency to justify disobedience by circumstances, a pattern that returns in 15:20–21.

verses.text: therefore I said, ‘Now the Philistines will come down on me to Gilgal, and I haven’t entreated the favor of the LORD.’ I forced myself therefore, and offered the burnt offering.”
verses.arminianNotes: Saul says he feared the Philistines would attack before he had “entreated the favor of the LORD,” so “I forced myself therefore.” Arminian readers note that Saul presents his act as reluctant piety. His concern to seek God’s favor was real, but he sought it in a way God had not appointed.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that Saul treats the sacrifice almost as a means of securing God’s help, rather than as worship offered in obedience. Samuel’s later word applies: “to obey is better than sacrifice” (15:22). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as warning against using religious acts to manage a crisis while setting aside God’s word.

verses.text: Samuel said to Saul, “You have done foolishly. You have not kept the commandment of the LORD your God, which he commanded you; for now the LORD would have established your kingdom on Israel forever.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says, “You have done foolishly,” for Saul has not kept the LORD’s commandment, “for now the LORD would have established your kingdom on Israel forever.” Arminian readers read the statement as a real conditional offer: Saul’s obedience would have led to a lasting dynasty, and his disobedience forfeited it.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers affirm Saul’s real responsibility and the genuine loss involved, while reading the statement within God’s overall purpose for the kingship, which the narrative goes on to locate in David (16:1). Shared ground: both traditions agree the verse concerns Saul’s kingdom and dynasty, that Saul is truly accountable, and that obedience to God’s word was the condition of his reign.

verses.text: But now your kingdom will not continue. The LORD has sought for himself a man after his own heart, and the LORD has appointed him to be prince over his people, because you have not kept that which the LORD commanded you.”
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel says, “your kingdom will not continue. The LORD has sought for himself a man after his own heart.” Arminian readers note that the judgment is grounded in Saul’s disobedience: “because you have not kept that which the LORD commanded you.” The rejection concerns his dynasty, and Saul continues to reign for years afterward.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the LORD has already chosen another, later identified as David, whom Paul recalls as “a man after my heart, who will do all my will” (Acts 13:22). Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as concerning the kingship and dynasty, not Saul’s eternal state, and both see in the “man after his own heart” the line that leads to the Messiah.

verses.text: Samuel arose, and went from Gilgal to Gibeah of Benjamin. Saul counted the people who were present with him, about six hundred men.
verses.arminianNotes: Samuel leaves for Gibeah, and Saul counts “about six hundred men.” Arminian readers note the stark result: Saul’s attempt to hold his army together by acting without Samuel ends with a force reduced to a few hundred. Disobedience did not achieve what it sought.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the dwindling army now resembles Gideon’s small band, but without the same trust in God. The stage is set for Jonathan’s exploit in chapter 14. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing the cost of Saul’s choice and the precarious position of Israel facing the Philistines.
